nodes.statement: Any affirmative infinitude proof supplies infinitely many distinct pairs (n,k), each satisfying k≥1, n≥2k, the full prime guard, and deficiency(n,k)=1.
Any affirmative finiteness proof for the second clause applies to the full admissible domain, with no k-range or congruence-class restriction.
COMPLETE TWO-CLAUSE CLOSE: determine both the infinitude of admissible deficiency-1 pairs and the finiteness of admissible deficiency->1 pairs.
The negation of clause (i) is finiteness of the admissible deficiency-1 pair set; the negation of clause (ii) is infinitude of the admissible deficiency->1 pair set.
COMPLETE NEGATIVE/MIXED CLOSE: negative answers are the literal negations of the two exact pair-set statements and both clauses are still determined.

For $n\geq 2k$ we define the deficiency of $\binom{n}{k}$ as follows. If $\binom{n}{k}$ is divisible by a prime $p\leq k$ then the deficiency is undefined. Otherwise, the deficiency is the number of $0\leq i<k$ such that $n-i$ is $k$-smooth, that is, divisible only by primes $\leq k$. Are there infinitely many binomial coefficients with deficiency $1$? Are there only finitely many with deficiency $>1$?

  let k : Nat := 3

    (∀ p : Nat, p.Prime → p ∣ Nat.choose n k → k < p))
